title: Egg washing and storage for home use
subtitle: When to wash, when not to, and how to store eggs from your own hens.
excerpt: Eggs laid at home arrive with a natural bloom that protects the contents. Washing removes that bloom and changes how the egg should be stored. Here is the UK guidance on washing, when it applies, and how to keep home eggs in the best condition.
sourceNotes: FSA guidance on home egg production and sale (2023). British Egg Information Service, How to store eggs at home. Poultry Club of Great Britain, egg cleaning guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin protective coating deposited on an egg's shell as it is laid. The bloom seals the shell pores, reduces moisture loss, and inhibits bacterial entry. Also called the cuticle.

content.text: An egg from your own hens has a natural

on its shell. This is not dirt. It seals the microscopic pores in the shell and is the main barrier against bacterial contamination. Washing removes it completely and changes how the egg behaves in storage.
The UK position on washing home eggs

For home use only (not for sale), the FSA advises that eggs should be collected daily and stored unwashed in a cool place. If an egg is visibly soiled and you want to clean it, dry-cleaning (brushing off dry dirt with a dry cloth) is preferable to washing. Once washed, the egg must be refrigerated and used within a few days, because the bloom is gone and the shell is more permeable.
Let any wet mud dry completely on the shell. Wet mud smears and is harder to remove than dry crusted mud.
Use a dry cloth, paper towel, or fine-grade sandpaper to rub the dirt away. Work in one direction to avoid spreading contamination.
Check the shell for cracks. Any cracked egg should be used immediately and cooked thoroughly, not stored.
If you do wash an egg
Use water that is at least as warm as the egg, ideally slightly warmer. Cold water causes the egg contents to contract and draws bacteria through the shell pores.
Rinse quickly under running water. Do not soak.
Dry thoroughly and refrigerate immediately. Use within three days.

Unwashed eggs with the bloom intact keep well at a steady cool temperature. A larder or pantry at 10 to 15°C is ideal. The refrigerator works too, but eggs absorb strong odours through the shell, so keep them away from pungent foods. At room temperature in summer (above 20°C) use unwashed eggs within two weeks; in a cool larder they will keep for four to five weeks from laying.

A fresh egg sinks and lies flat on the bottom of a bowl of cold water. As it ages, the air cell at the wide end grows and the egg tilts or floats. An egg standing upright on the bottom is still edible but should be used soon. A floating egg should be discarded.
